source_reviews.independent_solution: Work over neutral incidence/order/congruence geometry, with parallel meaning distinct disjoint coplanar lines. A quantifies over every line and every point and says at most one parallel; B quantifies over every admissible triple a,b,c. First prove neutrally that two perpendiculars to c at distinct feet are disjoint: an intersection would create a triangle with two right angles, whose right exterior angle contradicts the strict neutral exterior-angle theorem proved in 445. A implies B: let a meet c perpendicularly at P and b meet c obliquely at Q. If P=Q there is already a common point. Otherwise d, the perpendicular to c at Q, is parallel to a by the neutral lemma. If b were disjoint from a, both b and d would be parallels through Q to a; A would force b=d, contradicting obliqueness. B implies A: for an arbitrary line a and point X on a there are no disjoint parallels through X. For X outside a, drop c from X perpendicular to a and construct d through X perpendicular to c; d is parallel to a by the neutral lemma. Any b through X parallel to a intersects c at X. If b were oblique to c, B would force it to intersect a, a contradiction. Thus every such b is perpendicular to c and equals d by neutral perpendicular uniqueness. Both directions and all point cases are proved without assuming the conclusion. Concept 0 labels the same B statement E.

source_reviews.independent_solution: The task is an open request for examples of theorems whose proofs use A, not a unique exhaustive list. Example 1: for every pair of parallel lines cut by a proper transversal, corresponding and alternate interior angles are congruent and same-side interior angles are supplementary. Construct through the second intersection a line with the copied corresponding angle; 444 proves it parallel to the first neutrally, and A identifies it with the given second parallel through that point. Vertical angles and linear pairs supply the other angle forms. Example 2: every nondegenerate triangle has interior-angle sum 180 degrees. Draw through one vertex a parallel to the opposite side and use the A-dependent parallel-angle theorem to identify the other two interior angles with adjacent angles on the straight line. Example 3: every triangle exterior angle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles; combine that triangle-sum theorem with a linear pair. These exhibit precisely where A enters the proofs. The forward parallel-angle theorem must not be confused with 444's neutral converse. No claim about all possible proofs or historical attribution is required.

source_reviews.independent_solution: Valid examples with neutral proofs include: (1) every pair of vertical angles is congruent, since both are 180 degrees minus their common adjacent angle; (2) every triangle with AB=AC has congruent base angles, by neutral SSS comparing ABC with ACB; (3) distinct perpendiculars to one line are parallel, using perpendicular uniqueness at a shared foot and the neutral exterior-angle contradiction for distinct feet; (4) corresponding-angle congruence implies parallel lines under a proper transversal, by 444's neutral exterior-angle contradiction; (5) every triangle exterior angle is strictly greater than each remote interior angle, by 445's midpoint/extension/SAS/plane-order construction. Each example is universally quantified over admissible, nondegenerate configurations and avoids A. The mere occurrence of parallel lines or triangle angles in a theorem does not establish dependence on A; inequality must be distinguished from the A-dependent equality to the sum of remote angles.

source_reviews.independent_solution: For all distinct coplanar lines l,m cut by a proper transversal t at distinct P,Q, a congruent corresponding-angle pair implies that l,m are disjoint. Suppose they intersect at R off t. Congruence transfers to the other corresponding pairs by taking both supplements or both vertical angles. Choose both line rays toward R and the transversal direction from Q toward P. With Q-P-D on t, the corresponding-angle hypothesis gives angle RPD=angle PQR. In triangle PQR, RPD is exterior at P and PQR is a remote interior angle, so 445's neutral exterior-angle theorem gives angle RPD>angle PQR, contradiction. Hence l and m are parallel. This is the converse direction and requires neither A nor the forward theorem that parallel lines have equal corresponding angles. Distinct intersections and genuine corresponding-pair orientation are essential standard conventions.

source_reviews.independent_solution: For every nondegenerate triangle ABC, choose C-A-D and let epsilon=angle BAD. The claim is epsilon>angle ABC AND epsilon>angle ACB, each strictly; it is not an existential either/or. Let M be the midpoint of AB and extend C-M-N with CM=MN. SAS makes triangles BMC and AMN congruent, so angle MAN=angle ABC. N is opposite C across AB; M and B are on the same side of AC, and MN cannot cross AC because line CM meets AC only at C outside MN. Thus AN is strictly inside BAD and epsilon>angle ABC. To prove the other inequality, choose B-A-E, let K be the midpoint of AC and extend B-K-L with BK=KL. SAS gives angle CAL=angle ACB. L is opposite B across AC and on the C side of AB: KL cannot cross AB because line BK meets AB only at B outside KL. Thus AL is strictly inside CAE, giving angle CAE>angle ACB. CAE and BAD are vertical angles, hence epsilon>angle ACB. Only midpoint/extension construction, SAS, vertical angles, plane separation and strict angle inclusion/addition are used. No parallel axiom, parallel-angle equality, triangle-sum equality or exterior-equals-remote-sum formula is used.
